title: Shielding the Arteries of Finance: How Central Banks Keep Payments Flowing in Conflict
affiliations: Central Bank of Bahrain

detail.title: Shielding the Arteries of Finance: How Central Banks Keep Payments Flowing in Conflict
detail.abstract: Payment systems are a core pillar of national security. Modern economies run on digital payments, and any extended interruption translates rapidly into shortages, business closures, fiscal paralysis, and social unrest. In conflict conditions-war, sanctions, cyber warfare, or hybrid geopolitical confrontation-payment system resilience becomes critical infrastructure defense. This paper sets out a blueprint for how central banks and payment system operators can build and govern resilience across institutional, technological, and operational dimensions, drawing on recent experiences from Ukraine, Russia and   conflict-affected states. It presents a framework encompassing infrastructure redundancy, integrated cyber defense, liquidity resilience, cross-border contingency arrangements, and public confidence management. The  framework can be used for operational planning, board-level oversight, and supervisory coordination, supporting a more consistent, evidence-based approach to safeguarding payment continuity under the worst geopolitical conditions.

title: The Self-Driving Portfolio: Agentic Architecture for Institutional Asset Management
affiliations: Columbia University, Independent and Independent

detail.title: The Self-Driving Portfolio: Agentic Architecture for Institutional Asset Management
detail.abstract: Agentic AI shifts the investor's role from analytical execution to oversight. We present an agentic strategic asset allocation pipeline in which approximately 50 specialized agents produce capital market assumptions, construct portfolios using over 20 competing methods, and critique and vote on each other's output. A researcher agent proposes new portfolio construction methods not yet represented, and a meta-agent compares past forecasts against realized returns and rewrites agent code and prompts to improve future performance. The entire pipeline is governed by the Investment Policy Statement-the same document that guides human portfolio managers can now constrain and direct autonomous agents.

title: Material and Carbon Implications of Future Mobility Infrastructure Expansion around the World
affiliations: Universität für Bodenkultur Wien (BOKU), International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna, International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), Alpen Adria University - Institute of Social Ecology, International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) and University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna

detail.title: Material and Carbon Implications of Future Mobility Infrastructure Expansion around the World
detail.abstract: Accounting for one-third of the global stock of human-made physical assets, global mobility infrastructure is projected to expand significantly, especially in the Global South, requiring a substantial share of the remaining carbon budget. However, the resource use and carbon emissions associated with the anticipated expansion of roads, railways, and other mobility infrastructure, as well as the potential of mitigation measures, have so far not been explored systematically. Using high-resolution infrastructure and mobility data, we assess seven demand-and four supply-side circular economy and decarbonization measures to mitigate resource use and associated embodied CO₂ emissions. We find that without demand reduction, infrastructure stocks could double or triple by 2060, with cumulative emissions reaching 10 to 20 GtCO₂. We find that a global shift to rail would increase embodied emissions to 37 GtCO₂ due to carbon-intensive materials. Combining mobility reduction with enhanced recycling and industrial decarbonization can cut emissions by 63% while providing adequate global infrastructure. This would help to offset increases in emissions from public transport infrastructure expansion required to reduce operational emissions.

title: Rail as a Carbon Sink: Evidence from the COVID-19 Aviation Shock
affiliations: Vietnam National University - Ho Chi Minh City (VNU-HCM) - University of Economics and Law

detail.title: Rail as a Carbon Sink: Evidence from the COVID-19 Aviation Shock
detail.abstract: This paper uses the COVID-19 aviation collapse as a natural experiment to estimate the causal demand spillover from air to rail and its downstream effect on transport CO2 emissions across a 90-country panel from 1995 to 2023. Exploiting cross-country heterogeneity in shock severity, a first-difference panel estimator shows that air demand contraction raises rail ridership within the same country, while mediation analysis reveals that approximately 39 percent of the associated CO2 reduction flows through the rail diversion channel --- the first cross-country causal estimate of this environmental pathway. The modal shift response is strongly asymmetric: near-zero under normal conditions and far larger during acute supply disruptions, implying that discrete capacity constraints deliver greater decarbonisation dividends than gradual carbon pricing. The response is also substantially larger outside Europe, where rail capacity is less saturated, suggesting high environmental returns to rail investment in developing economies.

title: Monetary Sovereignty and Catastrophe Fiscal Capacity: Turkey, Japan, and the Limits of Disaster Self-Insurance

detail.title: Monetary Sovereignty and Catastrophe Fiscal Capacity: Turkey, Japan, and the Limits of Disaster Self-Insurance
detail.abstract: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) establishes that a government issuing its own floating-rate fiat currency faces no financial constraint on spending, only a real resource constraint. Yet the MMT literature has not systematically examined what this distinction implies for a sovereign’s capacity to absorb catastrophe losses, the fiscal shock that arises when a major natural disaster strikes and uninsured costs fall on the state. The concept of catastrophe fiscal capacity, introduced here,: a sovereign’s ability to finance disaster recovery without triggering a currency crisis, an inflation spiral, or a debt-sustainability panic. It argues that catastrophe fiscal capacity is determined not by the fiscal deficit or the debt-to-GDP ratio, but by the degree of monetary sovereignty a state commands. The paper operationalises this claim through a six-dimension monetary sovereignty index and applies it to a comparative analysis of Japan and Turkey, two seismically exposed countries at opposite ends of the monetary sovereignty spectrum. Using IMF WEO sectoral balances data, it demonstrates that Japan sustained a 9 per cent of GDP fiscal deficit across the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake with zero financial stress—no currency depreciation, no yield increase, no inflation—because full monetary sovereignty ensured frictionless transmission. In Turkey, the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake widened the deficit by 4.2 percentage points of GDP; the current account actually improved under CBRT tightening, yet the lira depreciated 30 per cent, revealing that for constrained issuers, exchange rates respond to dollarisation dynamics and financial structure rather than flow balances, and that financial amplification channels (KKM quasi-fiscal liabilities, corporate FX debt, inflationary pass-through) transform moderate fiscal impulses into macroeconomic crises. The paper draws three conclusions: MMT’s spectrum of monetary sovereignty can be operationalised as a framework for assessing sovereign catastrophe fiscal capacity; conventional development finance instruments such as sovereign catastrophe bonds impose unnecessary costs on governments with sufficient monetary sovereignty; and for constrained issuers, the operative constraint is not domestic fiscal space but the external balance, a real constraint that is financially intermediated and financially amplified.

title: AI and the Crisis of Question Competence: Entropy, Cognitive Misalignment, and the Limits of Prompt-Driven Intelligence

detail.title: AI and the Crisis of Question Competence: Entropy, Cognitive Misalignment, and the Limits of Prompt-Driven Intelligence

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become deeply embedded in institutional and economic decision-making, scholarly attention has largely focused on model alignment, safety, and capability. This paper argues that a structurally underexamined factor in AI failure is human question competence. Drawing on information theory, behavioral economics, and recent AI safety literature, the study conceptualizes inquiry as an entropy-modulating cognitive operation. Poorly structured questions increase interpretive entropy, degrade semantic coherence, and amplify epistemic instability. The paper formalizes Question Entropy, introduces a Question Competence Index (QCI), and models institutional entropy accumulation in recursive AI-mediated decision loops. It reframes alignment not solely as a model-centric problem but as a systemic interaction between inquiry architecture and probabilistic resolution. The crisis of question competence is therefore epistemic rather than technological, with implications for AI governance, education, and organizational design.

title: Generative AI and Business: A Review and Research Agenda

detail.title: Generative AI and Business: A Review and Research Agenda
detail.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI or GenAI) is an emerging and fast-growing technology with important consequences for workers, businesses, and society. GenAI is a subset of Machine Learning, which is a branch of Artificial Intelligence (AI) that not only analyzes data but also produces human-like output in response to users' prompts. These creative capabilities distinguish it from former iterations of AI, with distinctive and profound implications. Largely unknown before, GenAI became a household term in the fall of 2022 with the wide release and adoption of ChatGPT. Since then, GenAI has incited discussion and debate in many settings, including education, social media, and engineering. However, much uncertainty and confusion surrounds the topic, even with its widespread adoption. To gain a better understanding of the topic requires a brief overview to clarify some of the most pressing issues pertaining to GenAI and business introducing GenAI and what makes it different from traditional AI, highlighting its ability to produce data besides analyzing it. The generated data or the output that GenAI produces can be categorized as language-based, visual, auditory, and multimodal. Each category has applications in several fields that range from incremental to transformative. Use cases in customer service, sales and marketing, finance, healthcare, education, gaming, and operations are also relevant. Although much has been made of the benefits of using GenAI, there are also important challenges, particularly in terms of a program's design, technological limitations, and ethical and legal considerations.

title: Once Burned: Retail Crowd Behavior and Asymmetric Learning After Collective Market Losses

detail.title: Once Burned: Retail Crowd Behavior and Asymmetric Learning After Collective Market Losses
detail.abstract: We study retail investor crowd behavior following the COVID-19 market crash of February–March 2020, exploiting cross-sectional variation in collective retail losses to test whether prior crash losses distort how retail crowds process subsequent return signals. Using daily Robinhood popularity data combined with stock-level data, we construct a retail loss intensity measure that captures both the breadth of pre-crash retail ownership and the severity of the price decline experienced during the crash. We document a strong baseline asymmetry in retail crowd behavior: investors increase holdings in appreciating stocks but exit declining stocks at nearly twice the rate. More importantly, prior crash losses amplify this asymmetry in a manner consistent with a behavioral scarring effect — retail crowds become approximately three times more sensitive to subsequent negative return signals than to positive ones in high-loss stocks. This asymmetric learning pattern is concentrated in stocks with the highest pre-crash retail ownership, with null results in lower ownership quintiles serving as natural placebo tests. Our findings extend the disposition effect literature to the crowd level, suggesting that collective loss experience creates persistent asymmetries in how retail investors update their trading behavior in response to new information.

title: From Hierarchy to Humanity: uBuntu Leadership in Five African Countries and U.S Educational Contexts

detail.title: From Hierarchy to Humanity: uBuntu Leadership in Five African Countries and U.S Educational Contexts
detail.abstract: Employing Krippendorff's content analysis, I analyzed 13 articles about uBuntu and educational leadership to comparatively consider how uBuntu is applied in educational settings in Rwanda, Nigeria, South Africa, Malawi, and the United States. The research question is: What are the similarities and differences in how uBuntu is applied in educational leadership? The comparative content analysis revealed: 1). uBuntu as Relational and Ethical Leadership, 2). Contrast with Western/Colonial Models, 3). Education and Leadership Transformation, 4). Gender, Inclusion, and Exclusion, 5). uBuntu and Social Justice / Healing. Therefore, this comparative paper strives to examine the differences and similarities uBuntu applications for educational leadership.

title: Auxiliary Benefits and the Fiscal Sustainability of Social Security in an Aging Economy
affiliations: Otaru University of Commerce

detail.title: Auxiliary Benefits and the Fiscal Sustainability of Social Security in an Aging Economy
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of auxiliary benefits on the sustainability of Social Security in an aging economy. I develop a computable overlapping generations model with heterogeneous households in which individuals may be single or married, face marriage and divorce risks, and may become widowed, thereby explicitly incorporating auxiliary benefits into the analysis. Using the calibrated model, I simulate an aging economy to quantify the additional taxes required to sustain the Social Security system. The results show that auxiliary benefits significantly increase the fiscal burden and that the gap in required taxes between economies with and without auxiliary benefits widens as the population ages. This gap remains substantial even when the retirement age is raised. The analysis provides quantitative insights into the macroeconomic and fiscal effects of auxiliary benefits. Moreover, incorporating marriage and divorce risks is essential; otherwise, the fiscal impact of auxiliary benefits is overstated.

title: The Capacity Geometry of Global Trade: Polynomial-Time Routing in N P -Hard Disruption Regimes
affiliations: and Leeds Beckett University - Leeds Business School

detail.title: The Capacity Geometry of Global Trade: Polynomial-Time Routing in N P -Hard Disruption Regimes
detail.abstract:
We develop a geometric and optimization-based framework for analyzing resilience in global trade networks under heterogeneous disruptions. The model formulates trade flows as a constrained network allocation problem, where capacity constraints define a high-dimensional feasibility region whose structure is deformed by exogenous shocks. We show that, in realistic large-scale networks, strict feasibility is generically unattainable, leading to the collapse of classical resilience metrics. To address this, we introduce a penalized capacity geometry that yields well-posed recovery solutions and admits a tractable mean-field interpretation. 
Theoretical results establish existence, stability, and convergence properties of the penalized formulation, while numerical experiments on scale-free networks demonstrate its empirical robustness. Monte Carlo simulations reveal a fundamental trade-off between recovery magnitude and efficiency, as well as the endogenous emergence of bottleneck structures that concentrate flow along critical edges. These findings provide a unified framework for quantifying systemic resilience in complex trade systems and highlight the importance of soft-constrained optimization in high-dimensional disrupted environments.

title: Effectiveness of Trading Pauses: Evidence from the Tokyo Stock Exchange
affiliations: The University of Osaka and

detail.title: Effectiveness of Trading Pauses: Evidence from the Tokyo Stock Exchange
detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effect of single-stock trading pauses on market quality using tick-by-tick order book data from the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE). Our instrumental variable exploits the TSE's fixed yen-denominated triggering thresholds, which generate plausibly exogenous variation in the percentage distance to a trading pause across stocks with different price levels. Trading pauses significantly reduce post-event volatility, narrow quoted bid-ask spreads, and facilitate price discovery. Order-level analysis reveals the mechanism: during pauses, liquidity providers submit opposite-direction limit orders at aggressively priced levels that push the matching price toward reversal, generating the observed improvements. These effects are strongest for less frequently traded stocks, where incremental liquidity has the largest impact. However, the benefits are attenuated for highly volatile stocks with recent negative returns, particularly during broad market downturns.

title: The Aid Paradox: Why More Assistance Can Reduce Welfare
affiliations: and Consultant

detail.title: The Aid Paradox: Why More Assistance Can Reduce Welfare
detail.abstract: This paper develops a simple welfare framework showing that development assistance may reduce real household welfare in structurally rigid recipient economies. Aid operates as a sustained demand-side transfer. When firm entry and institutional adjustment are constrained, increased demand raises domestic prices faster than supply can expand. Incumbent producers capture rents, while households face a higher cost of consumption, generating a welfare reversal even when measured income rises. The model identifies a critical threshold for the elasticity of entry with respect to aid: aid improves welfare only if the supply response is sufficiently strong to offset the demand-driven increase in prices-a condition least likely to hold in economies receiving large and persistent aid flows. The mechanism differs from standard Dutch Disease accounts by operating through constrained entry and price-mediated redistribution rather than sectoral reallocation or growth effects and applies more broadly to sustained externally financed demand injections in low-adjustment environments.

title: For Shorter or Poorer: Attitudes Toward the Trade-Off between Poverty and Morality
affiliations: World Bank, University of Antwerp - Institute of Development Policy and World Bank

detail.abstract: Many policy decisions involve trade-offs between lives and livelihoods. We provide the first estimates for a new welfare parameter that expresses this trade-off in the longevity-poverty space. To do so, we conduct randomized survey experiments with 20,000 respondents across seven middle-and high-income countries. Both the median and mean responses imply that individuals are willing to spend no more than about two years in poverty to gain one additional year of life, sharply restricting the plausible range for this normative parameter. We show how these estimates can inform policy trade-offs related to long-run global development, pandemic responses, and climate change.

detail.abstract: This article examines how organizations can translate insights from cultural assessments into sustained, organization-wide transformation. Culture assessment must be embedded as an ongoing leadership discipline aligned with strategy rather than a reactive diagnostic tool and effective cultural transformation requires coordinated interventions across leadership behavior, talent systems, communication practices and organizational infrastructure. Key strategies include aligning leadership actions with desired values, embedding culture into hiring and onboarding, reinforcing norms through recognition and rewards, and equipping middle managers as culture carriers. Also important is psychological safety, continuous feedback and listening systems, continuous learning and alignment of policies, structures, and incentives with cultural objectives.

A Novel Design Paradigm for Behavioral and Relational Computing

detail.title:
Happiness-Oriented Technology Platforms
A Novel Design Paradigm for Behavioral and Relational Computing
detail.abstract: Digital platforms currently prioritize engagement over human flourishing. This paper proposes Happiness-Oriented Technology Platforms (HOTPs), a paradigm where system architecture explicitly promotes positive psychological states and relational trust. Drawing on flow theory and the Day Reconstruction Method, we argue that achieving flourishing requires relocating behavioral data capture from the application to the operatingsystem layer (or an intermediate operating layer). We present PlatOne-a behavioral operating layer-and Luanto, a domain-specific instantiation for tenant-landlord relationships. Together, they constitute a proof-ofconcept for the HOTP paradigm, with significant implications for platform design, digital well-being policy, and the future of organizational information systems.

title: Aging at the Very Top
affiliations: University of Bonn, Princeton University - Department of Economics and University of Bonn

detail.title: Aging at the Very Top
detail.abstract:
This paper documents that the age at which CEOs are appointed has risen sharply over the past several decades. Using newly assembled data covering a wide set of firms, we show that this increase is concentrated outside the largest listed firms and driven primarily by longer and more diverse external career paths prior to CEO appointment. These patterns are difficult to reconcile with explanations based on demographics, schooling, or tenure, and are instead consistent with a matching framework in which rising demand for generalist human capital leads firms to trade off peak ability for accumulated experience. We investigate the forces behind this shift. Using variation in consulting networks, we establish that firms place greater weight on diversified managerial experience as operating environments have become increasingly uncertain and complex. We also provide evidence for a supply-side response in which prospective CEOs broaden their skill portfolio as demand for generalist skills rises.

title: Taxing the Task: Automated Production, Fiscal Exposure, and the Case for Task-Level Taxation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Taxing the Task: Automated Production, Fiscal Exposure, and the Case for Task-Level Taxation
detail.abstract:
Modern fiscal systems are built on a foundational assumption: that economic production is organized around human labor, and that wages constitute a stable, observable tax base. This assumption is increasingly untenable. As artificial intelligence and robotics mature, production will be reorganized around automated task execution—a continuous, ambient process that operates outside the event-driven architecture of payroll taxation. This paper argues that the appropriate fiscal response is not a tax on robots as capital goods, but a recurring tax on automated task execution—the marginal unit at which machines substitute for human labor.

Drawing on the task-based production framework of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019, 2020), this paper develops a formal model in which a per-task tax on automated production shifts the automation threshold, generates a hump-shaped revenue function, and serves as an automatic fiscal stabilizer as the wage base erodes. The model yields an optimal differentiated rate structure grounded in task-level substitution elasticity and Pigouvian externality pricing, providing theoretical justification for graduated rate bands across task categories.

The paper further argues that task-level taxation addresses a deeper institutional gap: the absence of fiscal infrastructure for ambient economic processes. Just as advertising monetized the continuous attention captured by social media platforms, the task tax makes continuous automated production legible to the state. This framing extends naturally to developing economies, where task taxation may enable fiscal leapfrogging—formalizing robotic production in contexts where payroll infrastructure never existed. Implementation architecture, behavioral design, privacy-preserving enforcement mechanisms, and a human task credit system are discussed.

title: How Doctrine Texts Shape Distributed Leadership in High-Pressure Unmanned Environments：A Multi-Layer Semantic-Organizational-Training Analysis of an FPV Countermeasure Manual
affiliations: The University of Western Australia

detail.title: How Doctrine Texts Shape Distributed Leadership in High-Pressure Unmanned Environments：A Multi-Layer Semantic-Organizational-Training Analysis of an FPV Countermeasure Manual
detail.abstract: This study reconceptualizes Enemy Tactics for Using FPV Drones (with diagrams) and its associated countermeasures not merely as a tactical handbook, but as an organizational-cognitive mechanism through which leadership is codified, distributed, and normalized in practice. It addresses three closely connected questions: how doctrinal discourse organizes roles, prescribes actions, and defines constraints; how risk warnings, training requirements, and coordination norms are translated into signals of distributed leadership; and how textual discipline shapes organizational sensemaking, micro-level coordination, and the development of leadership capabilities.Methodologically, the study integrates directed content analysis, ruleenhanced sentence-function classification, semantic-cluster validation, and heterogeneous knowledge-graph modelling, using the 32-page FPV manual as its sole primary corpus. To ensure auditability, the datageneration pipeline is specified in eight stages: text extraction, cleaning, dual-level segmentation, codingontology construction, researcher coding, machine-assisted review, figure production, and alternativeexplanation auditing. The findings show that, at the first-order semantic level, the manual is dominated by countermeasure governance, technological capability, and organizational coordination, while at the sentencefunction level it is weighted most heavily toward description, command, and coordination. The Leadership Signal Index further suggests that the text privileges role allocation and behavioral discipline over heroic individual leadership, whereas psychological regulation and training density, although weaker in frequency terms, carry disproportionate interpretive significance. On this basis, the study proposes a four-stage mechanism-technological pressure, textual discipline, coordinative internalization, and distributed leadership formation-and argues that leadership development in high-pressure unmanned environments begins not with the expansion of personal charisma, but with the institutional internalization of perceptual responsibility, role coupling, alert obligations, and disciplinary structure that doctrine text preconfigures.

title: Belief Dispersion and Entrepreneurial Entry
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Belief Dispersion and Entrepreneurial Entry
detail.abstract:
When should a founder act on a strong belief about an opportunity, knowing that rivals assessing the same opportunity may hold very different views? This paper studies entry decisions when entrepreneurs hold heterogeneous beliefs about an opportunity's value and each founder knows only the range of views rivals might hold. In equilibrium, a founder enters only when their conviction exceeds a threshold set by anticipated rival optimism. The relationship between belief dispersion and entry is surprisingly rich: depending on the founder's conviction and the cost of entry, there may be no level of dispersion that supports entry, all levels may support it, or only a middle range may, so that an outside observer may see the most entry at intermediate levels of belief dispersion. When founders can delay, high dispersion that deters immediate entry need not prevent it altogether: the absence of rival action gradually reveals that competitors are less bullish than feared. Finally, not all conviction-building is equal. Validation that only the founder sees strengthens entry incentives fully, whereas validation visible to the whole market partly backfires by encouraging rivals. The paper formalises the intuition that entrepreneurial value comes not from optimism alone but from optimism that the founder anticipates rivals will not share, and derives predictions linking belief dispersion to entry patterns.

title: Information Treatments, Hypotheticals, and Event Studies: Comparative Estimates
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research, University of Macau and University of Reading

detail.title: Information Treatments, Hypotheticals, and Event Studies: Comparative Estimates
detail.abstract:
We study how consumer expectations respond to monetary policy announcements using a two-wave survey experiment around the September 2025 FOMC meeting. We compare three commonly used approaches to identifying causal effects on expectations: hypothetical ("vignette’’) scenarios, randomized control trials, and event studies. All three identification strategies yield qualitatively similar results: a rate cut reduces short- and long-run inflation expectations, raises expectations of economic activity, and lowers unemployment expectations. The estimated magnitudes are similar across the randomized controlled trial and event-study approaches, but relatively larger for vignette-based measures. Within-respondent comparisons further show that individuals who revise their expectations more in response to vignette scenarios also exhibit larger revisions following actual policy announcements and experimental information treatments.

title: The Architecture of Leverage: Structural Concentration and Competitive Moats in the AI Compute Supply Chain

detail.title: The Architecture of Leverage: Structural Concentration and Competitive Moats in the AI Compute Supply Chain

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, or experiments. All analyses are based on publicly available secondary sources such as regulatory filings, earnings call transcripts, patent databases, and industry reports. As such, formal ethics committee approval was not required.

detail.abstract:
The global artificial intelligence hardware ecosystem is frequently reduced to a GPU-centric narrative. This paper argues that such framing obscures the true architecture of competitive advantage in the AI compute supply chain. Through systematic analysis of regulatory filings (SEC Forms 20-F and 10-K), earnings call transcripts, patent portfolio data, and primary industry data, this paper maps the power dynamics across three foundational layers: advanced packaging (CoWoS), high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and advanced substrate materials (ABF). We introduce a three-tier taxonomy — Class A (genuine pricing power), Class B (capped cyclical upside), and Class C (narrative exposure without structural position) — grounded in four structural criteria and operationalized through a replicable composite scoring instrument, the Irreplaceability Index (IRI): technology scarcity, supply concentration, customer qualification barriers, and replacement cycle length. Quantitative analysis of TSMC's NT$291 billion customer prepayment liability (FY2024 20-F), SK Hynix's architectural lock-in via HBM4 customer-specific logic die design, and Ajinomoto's 95%+ ABF material market share demonstrates that value in the AI stack concentrates at nodes of irreplaceability, not nodes of revenue scale. 
This expanded version extends the analysis in three dimensions. First, a full vertical analysis maps the upstream equipment layer (ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research) and downstream substrate and OSAT tiers, providing a complete profit distribution topology anchored in FY2025 financial data. Second, a patent portfolio analysis characterizes three structurally distinct IP moat types across the three Class A nodes, drawing on LexisNexis PatentSight data, KnowMade hybrid bonding landscape analysis, and KIPRO institutional research — with the finding that SK Hynix's operational dominance in HBM is not matched by foundational legal protection in hybrid bonding, the critical technology for HBM4 and HBM5. Third, the demand origination structure is analyzed through the lens of $600+ billion in annual hyperscaler capital expenditure commitments for 2026, establishing the demand transmission mechanism and time-delay structure that propagates through the supply chain vertical.
The paper further stress-tests these moats against four disruption vectors — algorithmic memory compression (TurboQuant), HBM demand reversal mechanics, geopolitical concentration in Taiwan, and the material science transition toward glass substrates — and concludes that while current Class A moats are structurally robust through approximately 2027–2028, each carries identifiable expiration conditions with measurable milestone timelines.

title: Why Academia Can Never be "Just A Job" (And Why That is Actually Okay)

detail.abstract: The uncomfortable truth is that academia isn't a regular job, and pretending otherwise will not fix what is broken. A recent commissioned piece in Nature Human Behaviour titled "Academia Is Just a Job" by Laurel Raffington, struck a chord with burnt-out researchers everywhere (1). Her message? Clock in at 9 a.m., clock out at 5 p.m., and stop martyring yourself for science. Moreover, if you do, you will become both more productive and more content with your academic life. Like many of us, I was initially attracted by the pitch's simplicity and timeliness, at a time when I was swamped with administrative work and rushing to submit a paper revision, often working weekends to keep up with my teaching. But here is where I draw the line, based on firsthand lessons learned throughout my career. Forcing academic work into a conventional 9-to-5 mold isn't just impractical, it's a recipe for mediocrity. The answer isn't to pretend academia is like working at an insurance company. It's to design smarter policies that honor both human wellbeing and the chaotic, serendipitous nature of discovery.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how government venture capital (GVC) affects firm growth and financing in small and medium-sized enterprises. Using matched panel data for Swedish firms over 2008-2020, we evaluate impacts on employment, sales, equity, and debt. GVC-backed firms expand employment almost immediately after investment, while sales growth follows with a lag of two to three years. GVC participation also strengthens firms' equity positions and improves access to bank credit, consistent with certification and balance-sheet channels that alleviate financial constraints. Importantly, the positive impacts are concentrated in metropolitan and innovation-dense regions. Despite receiving a disproportionately large share of GVC funding due to regional allocation rules, rural and peripheral regions display notably weaker effects, suggesting that local ecosystem depth moderates program effectiveness. These findings highlight the dual role of GVC as both growth finance and a mechanism for reducing capital-market imperfections, while raising policy questions about the efficiency of geographically earmarked allocation. These findings demonstrate that GVC generates genuine financial additionality by improving both equity and credit access.

title: The Coordination Age
affiliations: Woxsen University and

detail.title: The Coordination Age
detail.abstract: This article introduces Coordination Capacity (Ψ)-the geometric mean of cognitive, emotional, metacognitive, and relational sub-components-as the master variable of human performance from individual decisions to civilisational governance. The thesis is that the binding constraint on human flourishing is no longer information, intelligence, or capital; it is the capacity to coordinate. Three theorems establish a phase transition at Ψ* ∈ [0.35, 0.42] below which selfcorrection becomes structurally impossible (Theorem 1), prove that no additive model generates the four required properties (Theorem 2), and derive path-dependent cascades below threshold (Theorem 3). A Fokker-Planck extension with Kramers escape-rate theory explains behavioural volatility as threshold-mediated stochastic fluctuation. The architecture produces the same five The Coordination Age-Rodriguez emergent properties at individual, dyadic, group, institutional, market, democratic, and civilisational scales wherever four structural conditions are satisfied. Empirical grounding spans four evidence levels: Level 1 (published, independently replicated)six neural coupling pathways with effect sizes ranging from d = 0.3 to 0.8; Level 2 (published, not yet replicated within the framework)-the ego depletion reanalysis demonstrating a phasetransition artefact; Level 3 (preliminary, by the present author)-power-mean estimation (N = 26,600) favouring geometric over arithmetic aggregation (ΔAIC = 28.4), Market Coordination Index with phase-transition breakpoint at MCI = 0.41, and real-time crisis prediction during the 2026 Iran-Middle East conflict achieving 91%+ directional accuracy against a 33% chance baseline; Level 4 (theoretical predictions)-Kramers escape-rate derivation, civilisational immune deficiency, and six AI degradation mechanisms. The framework subsumes five theoretical traditions-prospect theory, dual-process theory, ecological rationality, social identity theory, and ego depletion-and generates twenty falsifiable predictions with explicit disconfirmation criteria. Five concrete implementation protocols with instruments, costs, and pilot designs are specified. If the core predictions fail, the theory fails; this article specifies exactly what failure would look like.

title: The Individual Power User and the Missing Middle: Pricing Deserts, Shadow Stacks, and the Commercial-Professional Zoning Failure in AI Platform Economics

detail.abstract:
The AI platform industry has built two subscription tiers: a $20 consumer offering and a $200+ enterprise suite. Between them sits a structurally significant population of sophisticated independent professionals with no purpose-built product. This paper identifies that population, the Individual Power User (IPU), estimates its revenue value, and makes the structural case that the gap is correctable. Drawing on Lead User innovation theory (von Hippel, 1986), two-sided platform economics (Rochet & Tirole, 2003), and original compute-unit margin modeling, the paper argues that the $20-to-$200 Pricing Desert constitutes a Commercial-Professional Zoning Failure carrying an estimated $1.3 billion to $3.7 billion in addressable professional spend currently fragmented across competing platforms, from an estimated 1.5 to 5 million AI-enabled independent professionals.

Three constructs drive the analysis. The Strategic ARPU Bridge defines a $60-$120 per month pricing bracket, the IPU Capture Zone. Unit economics modeling indicates IPUs on $20 tiers generate a TMR of 0.25-0.36x (Severe Margin Drain), while the same users on $90-$120 tiers generate 1.13-2.18x (High-Margin Asset). Structural Fencing separates the Individual Pro tier, built for power and velocity, from the Enterprise tier, built for institutional governance, mitigating cannibalization risk.

The zoning analogy anchors the argument: AI platforms have written pricing ordinances for Residential (consumer) and Industrial (enterprise) use while leaving the Professional tier unzoned. The correction is a deliberate zoning decision: create the tier, price it at $60-$120, fence it from enterprise, and capture the Shadow Stack spend currently flowing to competitors. The paper concludes with a validation framework and the strategic imperative for 2026: zone correctly before a competitor does.

title: Free at Last? The Contractual Theory of the Corporation and the New Maryland Officer-Director Liability Provisions
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School and University of Illinois College of Law (deceased)

detail.title: Free at Last? The Contractual Theory of the Corporation and the New Maryland Officer-Director Liability Provisions

publicationDetails.detailsText: George Mason Legal Studies Research Paper No. LS
publicationDetails.journalName: Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Baltimore Law Review, Vol. 18, pp. 352-367 (1988)

detail.abstract:
Perhaps the most significant debate in corporation law today concerns the extent to which corporations and their shareholders should be free to order internal corporate relations, in particular the fiduciary duties of officers and directors. One view is that the corporation is a set of private contractual relationships and, as such, should be no less amenable to private ordering than other contracts. The competing view holds that the corporation differs fundamentally from a conventional contract and, as such, should be subject to mandatory rules. This latter, or anticontractualist, position derives in part from the now outmoded original view of the corporation as a creation or concession of the state.

The debate on the nature of the corporation has been brought to a head by a number of recent developments, particularly the explosion in takeover activity and the so-called "crisis" in director liability insurance. The latter development has spurred state legislatures to enact one or both of two different types of corporation law provisions. The first type of provision explicitly authorizes corporations to adopt by shareholder vote charter provisions limiting director liability. The second type of provision changes the liability rules by legislative fiat without action by the shareholders. Maryland has recently added both types of provisions.

The director liability crisis and the statutes that have been enacted to resolve it present a perfect opportunity to demonstrate both the strengths of a coherent contractual theory of the corporation and the operation of such a theory in practice. The liability crisis, if there is one, may have occurred because the parties to corporations have not been given free rein in drafting their managerial contracts. Offering more contractual freedom to shareholders, therefore, will go a long way toward solving the director liability problem. But state legislatures should learn a lesson from this crisis and fully accept the implications of the contractual theory. Because the new Maryland provisions, like similar provisions in other states, do not fully accept the implications of the contractual theory, they raise significant practical and theoretical problems.

This article examines the recent Maryland statutory changes from the perspective of the contractual theory of the corporation. In general, it discusses how the two types of provisions adopted in Maryland raise different types of concerns under the contractual theory of the corporation. Part II briefly outlines the contractual theory of the corporation and its implications for contracting in and out of fiduciary duties. Part III discusses the new Maryland shareholder option provision and demonstrates that this type of provision is consistent with the contract theory except to the extent that it limits the shareholders' options. Part IV examines the new Maryland indemnification provision which raises serious concerns both under the contract theory and the Contract Clause of the United States Constitution because it amounts to a retroactive change in the shareholders’ contract. Finally, Part V offers concluding observations.

title: Queue Visibility Decisions in Customer-Intensive Services
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), , Tilburg University and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Queue Visibility Decisions in Customer-Intensive Services

publicationDetails.journalName: HKUST Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Managers of customer-intensive services face a speed-quality trade-off: increasing the service speed improves productivity while reducing customers' perceived value of service quality. Many studies have explored the operational implications of such a trade-off; yet, the role of queue information, another key factor that shapes customers' queueing behaviors, remains underexplored in this context. We find that under exogenous service prices, disclosing the queue length is more profitable when the base value of the service is low and service quality is highly sensitive to service speed. Moreover, disclosing the queue length may lead to lower service qualities as opposed to not disclosing the queue length. Under endogenous prices, disclosing the queue length remains favorable in a similar parameter regime, but in this regime, it leads to higher service qualities as opposed to not disclosing the queue length. Collectively, the quality contrast highlights the critical role of queue visibility and flexible pricing in managing customer-intensive services.

title: Does AI Investment Really Improve Equity Performance? AI Job Creation and Firm Value: Lessons from the S&P 500
affiliations: , Institute for Policy Research (IPR), University of Bath and University of Bath - Institute for Policy Research

detail.title: Does AI Investment Really Improve Equity Performance? AI Job Creation and Firm Value: Lessons from the S&P 500
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of the creation of AI job vacancies on firm value within the S&P 500 firms. Our study highlights the role of AI adoption and strategic investments in human capital. With a unique dataset from Lightcast and Compustat, we analyse more than 3.4 million job spanning from 2022Q3 to 2024Q1. Our findings reveal a significant positive relationship between AI job postings and firm value, measured through Tobin's Q (0.27%), Return on Equity (ROE) and Return on Assets (ROA) metrics. Firms advertising AI-related roles signal their commitment to innovation, aligning workforce strategies with technological advancements, which investors perceive as a driver of competitive advantage and growth. Robustness tests, including propensity score matching and instrumental variable approaches, confirm the validity of these findings. Furthermore, we create and index based on the AI jobs adverts per firm where our results also show that firms, independently of the sector, that have more AI job postings have a significant positive association with its firm value. Our research contributes to understanding how AI talent acquisition influences firm valuation and market perceptions, offering novel insights into workforce dynamics and technological innovation.

title: Portfolio Optimization and Rate-Distortion Theory: A Unified Information-Theoretic Framework
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Portfolio Optimization and Rate-Distortion Theory: A Unified Information-Theoretic Framework
detail.abstract:
We develop an information-theoretic perspective on portfolio optimization by interpreting portfolio construction as a constrained compression of return information.
For Gaussian returns, we show that the mean–variance frontier admits a natural rate–distortion representation once portfolio variance is viewed as distortion and the entropy of the portfolio return is viewed as an information complexity measure. This yields a variational reformulation of Markowitz optimization in which return, risk, and informational complexity appear in a single objective. We then study spectral decompositions of the covariance matrix, obtaining a reverse-waterfilling interpretation of dimensionality reduction in portfolio design, and we analyze mutual-information regularization as a complexity penalty that modifies effective risk aversion. We also discuss asymptotic links with growth-optimal allocation, robust portfolio selection under KL ambiguity, and iterative computational schemes inspired by Blahut–Arimoto. The paper therefore does not claim an exact identity between all classical portfolio problems and Shannon rate–distortion theory; rather, it establishes a mathematically tractable bridge that clarifies when the analogy is exact, when it is variational, and when it is only asymptotic.

title: Signaling Demand via Queue Visibility
affiliations: , Tilburg University, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Signaling Demand via Queue Visibility

publicationDetails.journalName: HKUST Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We consider a queueing system in which customers' arrival rate is uncertain and the realized arrival rate is the server's private information. The server utilizes this information asymmetry to devise queue disclosure strategies, signal demand information to customers, shape their beliefs and influence their joining behaviors so as to maximize the steady-state throughput. Using a signaling game framework, we identify a new equilibrium that can only exist under asymmetric demand information: the server conceals the queue length when the arrival rate is high and reveals the queue length otherwise. We also show that the usual complete-information equilibrium that reveals the queue length when the arrival rate is high and conceals the queue length otherwise is never a signaling equilibrium under asymmetric information. These results remain valid even if the server plays randomized queue disclosure strategies. We also find that compared with the complete-information case, there exists a non-negligible parameter regime of arrival rates in which the server's long-run throughput gets improved from signaling. This is especially true when the server has limited waiting space to accommodate queueing customers. Our findings provide actionable insights for service firms to manage demand-sensitive queueing systems. Our results highlight the strategic role of queue visibility in optimizing the system throughput, offering practical guidance for designing queue disclosure polices in environments with uncertain demands.

title: Generative AI Use in Entrepreneurship: An Integrative Review and an Empowerment-Entrapment Framework
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Tsinghua University and

detail.title: Generative AI Use in Entrepreneurship: An Integrative Review and an Empowerment-Entrapment Framework
detail.abstract: Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment-Entrapment Framework to understand how GenAI can both empower and entrap entrepreneurs, highlighting GenAI's role as a double-edged sword at each stage of the entrepreneurial process. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality but introduce hallucinations and training data biases; boost entrepreneurial self-efficacy but heighten entrepreneurial overconfidence; increase functional breadth but decrease relational embeddedness; and boost productivity but fuel "workslop" and erode critical thinking, learning, and memory. Moreover, we identify core features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. We also explore boundary conditions (e.g., entrepreneurs' metacognition, domain expertise, and entrepreneurial experience) that shape the magnitude of these effects. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and the Empowerment-Entrapment Framework offer practical implications for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically throughout the entrepreneurial process while managing its risks.

detail.abstract:
This paper articulates a novel axiomatized structural framework for analyzing irreversible industrial state transitions in capital-intensive systems, particularly within emerging energy–compute sectors. While traditional industrial entry models are grounded in optimization under rational expectations and smooth equilibrium adjustment, industries characterized by high sunk costs, infrastructural rigidity, and capital indivisibilities frequently exhibit threshold effects, discontinuous transitions, and asymmetric recovery dynamics that challenge conventional marginal analysis.

To formalize these structural features, the study introduces a Gate-based feasibility operator defined over a structured state vector incorporating capital intensity, cost structure, infrastructural coupling, and exogenous constraints. Viability holds if and only if predefined threshold conditions are satisfied, generating a discrete partition of the state space into PASS, HOLD, EXIT, and FAIL regions. The framework integrates a feasibility margin measuring structural distance from critical thresholds, a transition dominance parameter evaluating sustainability under perturbations, and a hysteresis variable embedding path dependence and irreversible collapse persistence directly into the transition mechanism.

By unifying threshold adjudication, hysteresis, and operator-based feasibility within a coherent axiomatic structure, the model extends industrial organization theory toward a complexity-consistent representation of industrial transition and succession dynamics. The resulting architecture contributes to the theoretical foundations of energy economics and infrastructure economics, providing a formal decision framework for policy evaluation and investment adjudication in infrastructure-intensive regimes governed by high fixed costs and constrained adaptability.

detail.abstract: We investigate how collective reputations influence foreign stock prices after outbreaks of corporate misconduct. We find that investors in the U.S. stock market penalize not only misconduct firms but also other foreign firms from the same country, especially among those from more trustworthy countries. The effect is more pronounced for foreign firms facing greater informational frictions, such as severe information asymmetry and weaker financial credibility, or operating in weaker institutional environments. Our findings suggest that the investors factor in a “trust premium” of foreign stocks, but they withdraw this premium when a country’s trustworthiness is compromised by its affinity firm’s misconduct.

title: The Artificial Intelligence Commission
affiliations: Emory University School of Law

detail.title: The Artificial Intelligence Commission

declarations.funderStatement: Professor Ajunwa's work has been founded by a diversity of sources: Including the National Science Foundation (NSF), Microsoft, The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (RWJF), and the MacArthur Foundation.

contentType.other: Accepted for publication. Forthcoming in the Georgetown Law Journal

detail.abstract: As history shows, the law has generally lagged technological developments and this comes at a cost. Although some applaud the (impending) demise of the Anthropocene, the breakneck speed of the development of A.I. technologies introduces legal quandaries such as the circumscription of due process, equal protection, and equal opportunity. Centralized legal interventions, rather than piecemeal state legislation, are necessary to ensure that A.I. technologies do more good than harm. This Article proposes the Artificial Intelligence Act which would create The Artificial Intelligence Commission ("A.I. Commission"), a federal agency dedicated to establishing and enforcing legal standards for the safe development and deployment of A.I. technologies. Unlike much earlier calls for a "Federal Search Commission," an "FDA for algorithms" or a "Robot commission," this proposed agency is more comprehensive and has teeth. Addressing the argument that the fast pace of A.I. development could render AI regulation a futile game of whack-a-mole, the Article proposes a nimble structure that is adaptable to any future A.I. developments. The Article's contributions are multifold: Part I of the Article details the need for the A.I. Commission, focusing on how A.I. technologies have already been deputized for governmental functions, how they impact consumer safety, and how they may widen the gulf of inequality. Part II of the Article discusses design lessons to be gleaned from the history of extant federal agencies. Deploying those lessons, Part III sketches key provisions of the A.I. Commission Act and also describes the agency's structure, purview, and charge. Part IV provides historical examples of legislation spurring innovation to rebut the regulatory dodge that regulation stifles innovation and parses First Amendment legal arguments against AI regulation.

detail.abstract: AI is widely framed as an inevitable driver of workforce disruption, yet observed labor outcomes vary sharply across organizations, industries, and diffusion stages. We argue that this heterogeneity is driven less by AI capability than by adoption depth: the joint alignment of organizational embedding and practitioner mastery. Using U.S. worker-level microdata spanning 2015-2025 (N = 869,273), we document (i) a conservative reduced-form AI exposure wage premium, (ii) a strong intensity gradient, (iii) pronounced education-based amplification consistent with human-AI complementarity, and (iv) nonlinear diffusion-stage dynamics. We formalize adoption depth as a complementarity structure and show that the empirical patterns are consistent with regime transition predictions. The study integrates organizational complementarity theory and labor economics while providing a scalable foundation for crosscountry institutional and policy extensions.

detail.abstract: Tax data has been used to argue that Malta has an inordinately high dependence on low wages, with the average wage significantly below that indicated by official statistics. Administrative data are a very useful source, but they must be used with caution as they do not conform to international statistical definitions. Due to high labour turnover, tax data for many full-time workers do not cover a whole year, but just some months. A more standardised wage distribution that considers persons with the same length of employment shows a significantly different picture; with very low wages five times less prevalent and the average wage a quarter higher than quoted in the press. The degree of wage inequality is also much less pronounced, though over time it has risen, probably reflecting higher labour participation, particularly among women and persons previously on benefits.

title: Toward a Theory of AI Disruption Resilience: Constructing the AI Resilience Index (AIRX)
affiliations: University of Wollongong

detail.title: Toward a Theory of AI Disruption Resilience: Constructing the AI Resilience Index (AIRX)
detail.abstract: Despite the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on competitive dynamics, the strategic management literature lacks a unified theoretical framework to explain why some firms sustain competitive performance through technological disruptions while others falter. This paper develops such a framework by introducing the concept of AI resilience and proposing the AI Business Resilience Index (AIRX) as its operationalization. Drawing on Schumpeterian creative destruction theory, the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities, and the emerging economics of AI, I define AI resilience as the capacity of a firm to maintain its risk-adjusted financial performance following exogenous AI-related shocks. I argue that AI resilience is a latent, multidimensional construct that manifests through five observable firm-level attributes: operational stability, margin consistency, innovation intensity, revenue durability, and structural AI insulation. The paper develops ten testable propositions linking each AIRX component to firm-level outcomes under conditions of AI-driven disruption, and delineates the boundary conditions under which AI resilience is more or less consequential.

title: The Epistemic Tension Metric: Quantifying Model Breakdown Before It Happens
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Epistemic Tension Metric: Quantifying Model Breakdown Before It Happens
detail.abstract: I propose a measurable indicator of systemic fragility-the epistemic tension δ-that rises when predictive models become decoupled from the reality they claim to represent. Unlike traditional risk metrics, δ captures the probability of unprecedented events by measuring four structural features: anomaly frequency, model homogeneity, structural complexity, and behavioral tension. Retrospective application to five major crises (1929, 1987, 2000, 2008, 2020) shows that δ > 0.8 consistently precedes systemic collapse, while conventional models assign near-zero probability to the realized outcomes. Prospective application to artificial intelligence in 2026 yields δ ≈ 0.875, suggesting immediate precautionary measures are warranted despite high modeled benefits. I outline governance architectures that operationalize δ-based decision regimes, emphasizing resilience over prediction.

title: Suicide Is Not the Problem: A Unified Framework for Addressing Adverse Childhood Experience Outcomes in American Indian and Alaska Native Populations

detail.title: Suicide Is Not the Problem: A Unified Framework for Addressing Adverse Childhood Experience Outcomes in American Indian and Alaska Native Populations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: No funders.

detail.abstract: Suicide is not a categorically distinct phenomenon requiring a categorically distinct intervention system. It is the terminal position on a single behavioral escalation spectrum driven by a body budget deficit produced at the population level through colonial destruction of the Dunbar-scale relational architecture that historically maintained individual nervous system regulation across generations. Drawing on Felitti's Adverse Childhood Experience Study epidemiology, Barrett's predictive processing framework, Sapolsky's stress physiology, LeDoux's dual-pathway model of threat response, Dunbar's social brain hypothesis, and four decades of executive leadership in Alaska Native health and governance organizations, this paper proposes a unified theoretical framework with three original contributions. First, a selection mechanism grounded in Population Attributable Risk as a behavioral menu: the nervous system selects from probabilistic relief options without conscious awareness, shaped by developmental accessibility and availability. Second, an escalation dynamic, driven by deepening deficit and diminishing yield, with suicide as a terminal position rather than a categorical phenomenon. Third, an extended Five Whys root cause analysis reaching to Why 9, epigenetic intergenerational transmission of amygdala threat calibration: with a tenth why addressing the institutional body budget conditions that have prevented interventions from reaching this depth. No existing intervention in the American Indian and Alaska Native suicide prevention literature operates below Why 4. The ultimate therapeutic goal is the reduction of baseline activation level through Dunbar relational architecture restoration, creating conditions in which a brief early-phase cortical interception window, the interval between amygdala initiation and full glucocorticoid cascade completion during which sympathetic arousal may be attenuated through somatic intervention, becomes accessible. The Shaman's Trail intervention framework (Anderson, 2026) is proposed as the first architecture explicitly designed to address the causal chain from Why 5 through Why 9. Implications for research, policy, and clinical protocol design are discussed.

title: Graph Coloring as Hierarchical Constraint Satisfaction: A Recursive Cube Approach to Chromatic Number
affiliations: University of Patras

detail.title: Graph Coloring as Hierarchical Constraint Satisfaction: A Recursive Cube Approach to Chromatic Number
detail.abstract: The graph coloring problem-determining whether a graph can be colored with k colors such that no adjacent vertices share the same color-is one of Karp's original 21 NP-complete problems and a fundamental challenge in combinatorial optimization. This paper extends the recursive cube validation framework, previously developed for Sudoku and Boolean Satisfiability, to graph coloring. We introduce the color cube, a three-dimensional binary array of dimensions n × k × m where n is the number of vertices, k is the number of colors and m is the number of edges (constraints). Each entry C 0 [v][c][e] = 1 iff assigning color c to vertex v satisfies the constraint imposed by edge e. By lifting the fundamental graph coloring constraints to operate on this cube and applying recursive validation, we obtain a hierarchy C 0 , C 1 ,. .. , C D where each level processes a smaller constraint problem. We prove that the recursion depth satisfies D = O(log n), that each level reduces ambiguity by a constant fraction and that total time complexity is polynomial in the graph size. The permanent cascade D-1 k=0 perm(M k) = 1 for uniquely colorable graphs reveals the same mechanism of complexity dissolution observed in previous applications. This generalization establishes that the recursive constraint principle applies universally to graph coloring, providing a polynomialtime algorithm for determining chromatic number and constructing optimal colorings.

detail.abstract: The impending arrival of superintelligent AI systems poses an unprecedented challenge to human institutions: how can governance structures that oversee self-improving gents remain aligned with evolving human values when those  agents will rapidly and irreversibly surpass their regulators in capability? This paper introduces Recursive eta-Governance (RMG), a formal framework that embeds self-stabilizing, provably aligned meta-level institutions capable of governing lower-level systems—including AI agents—through endogenous recursion. Drawing on mechanism design, category theory, typed lambda calculus, and the scalable oversight literature, we define a recursive language for governance protocols, establish a minimal axiom system, and prove key properties: stability, alignment preservation under bounded capability growth, compositional modularity, and non-corruptibility under adversarial coalition pressure. We demonstrate applicability through lightweight formal simulations and four conceptual case studies: the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, corporate board governance, and the failure modes of decentralized autonomous organizations. Unlike static external oversight models, RMG creates an adaptive, self-correcting governance layer that co-evolves with the systems it regulates, guided at every step by formally verified alignment invariants. This work establishes the foundational theory for a new field of recursive institutional engineering, offering a mathematically grounded pathway to safe long-term human flourishing amid transformative AI. All analysis is conducted with zero-budget tools, making it fully replicable by any independent researcher.

detail.abstract: Breathwork is widely promoted as a regulatory practice capable of calming the nervous system, releasing trauma and restoring emotional balance. While its therapeutic potential is well documented in experiential contexts, the long-term effects of repeated high intensity practice remain insufficiently examined. This paper explores the hypothesis that sustained autonomic activation and repeated emotional disinhibition may lower inhibitory thresholds and recalibrate baseline emotional reactivity in certain individuals. It argues that the same mechanisms that facilitate access to suppressed material may also sensitize anger pathways, reduce buffering capacity and increase volatility when activation outpaces integration. Rather than dismissing breathwork's benefits, this analysis calls for mature scrutiny of its threshold effects, particularly where families observe subtle but measurable shifts in tolerance and restraint.

detail.title: What’s in a Name? A Definition and Theoretical Integration of Cryptomarketing
detail.abstract: the term "cryptomarketing" has recently emerged among practitioners and academics to denote activities that use decentralized technologies to transform, improve, and supplement existing marketing strategies. in this commentary article, we resolve common confusions about the term's definition and illustrate how blockchain's idiosyncrasies enable marketing activities that have hitherto not been possible. We suggest ways to integrate cryptomarketing into nine theories frequently used in marketing research and propose exemplary research questions as starting points. in summary, we show why an informed academic debate on cryptomarketing will be valuable to scholars and practitioners.

title: Balancing between Utilization, Waiting Times and Service Equity in Outpatient Department: A Semi-Open Queuing Network Approach

detail.title: Balancing between Utilization, Waiting Times and Service Equity in Outpatient Department: A Semi-Open Queuing Network Approach
detail.abstract: Achieving an optimal balance between resource utilization, patient waiting times, and serviceequity is critical to patient satisfaction in hospital Outpatient Departments (OPDs). Patientscheduling significantly impacts this balance, particularly in multi-stage systems with heterogeneous patient classes, no-show rates, and returning patients. The traditional First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) policy, while efficient under light loads, proves ineffective and inequitable under high-feedback intensity. We model the OPD as a multistage system with endogenous feedback using a Semi-Open Queuing Network (SOQN) framework and evaluate the performance of eight prioritization policies, including static and state-dependent dynamic rules across nine Operating Environments (OE) defined by patient mix and no-show rates. Results show that policy performance is conditioned by OEs rather than being universally optimal. State-dependent dynamic policies prove more robust than static rules as they respond better to queue conditions, dampen congestion spillovers, reduce mean and extreme delays, and improve service equity. Experiments using real-life multi-specialty hospital data suggest that patient arrivals may be over-dispersed and heavy-tailed rather than Poisson. In such cases, dynamic policies effectively mitigate delays by handling episodic clustered arrivals. By aligning priority policies with observed OEs, managers can improve satisfaction, enhance fairness, and achieve resilient performance without requiring additional clinical resources.

title: A Modular, Decentralised Architecture as an Alternative to Monolithic Language Models -A Conversation Starter

detail.title: A Modular, Decentralised Architecture as an Alternative to Monolithic Language Models -A Conversation Starter
detail.abstract: This paper proposes PublicAI a modular, decentralised AI architecture in which large numbers of small specialist models, each capped at a configurable parameter limit, are organised into a navigable hierarchical tree and collectively produce outputs that can match or exceed monolithic general-purpose models on domain-specific tasks. The architecture is designed to be crowdcontributed, hardware-accessible, and owned by no single entity. This is explicitly a conversation starter, not a finished specification. The architecture presented here has known drawbacks, open engineering problems, and unresolved governance questionsdocumented honestly in Section 6. The intent is to invite critique, collaboration, and improvement from researchers, engineers, and domain practitioners. This paper draws on concepts from the Transformer architecture [1], Retrieval-Augmented Generation [2], Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [3], federated learning [4], and the PageIndex hierarchical document navigation approach [5]. Where these concepts are used, they are cited.

title: The Inefficient Pricing of News
affiliations: University of Melbourne, Yale SOM,  and University of Melbourne

detail.title: The Inefficient Pricing of News
detail.abstract:
The stock market fails to efficiently process information in news text (Chen et al., 2026). But news itself is highly predictable by prevailing stock characteristics, which complicates inferences about market efficiency. After purging news of its predictable content, the resulting “news shocks” more than double the monthly return predictive power of raw news, and they continue to significantly predict returns up to 18 months ahead. The magnitude and longevity of the news shock anomaly is larger than every anomaly in the Jensen et al. (2022) universe. The news shock anomaly derives from negative-tone and quantitative topics to which investors underreact and from high-attention and ambiguous topics to which investors overreact.

title: The Political Economy of Financial Crises
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Utah State University - Huntsman School of Business

detail.title: The Political Economy of Financial Crises
detail.abstract:
Financial crises remain a recurrent feature of modern economies despite evidence that many are predictable and preventable. This chapter discusses how financial instability often reflects a political equilibrium rather than purely technocratic shortcomings. Contrasting economic and political perspectives on regulation, the chapter emphasizes how policymakers shape financial rules in ways that favor politically-influential groups but result in financial vulnerability. Key mechanisms include restricted bank chartering, safety nets, credit subsidies, and sovereign borrowing. Political forces also shape crisis management. Delayed interventions, selective support, and constrained policy responses can deepen and prolong crises. Together, these dynamics help explain the persistent and foreseeable nature of financial instability across time, legal origins, political structures, and institutional contexts. Instead of seeing financial crises as arising from an unavoidable vulnerability to external shocks they are better seen as a mirror of the societies in which they occur, reflecting their political structures, vying constituencies, cultural preferences, and blind spots.
